newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swede accused by Russia as spy goes into hiding.
newsitem.headline: Swede accused by Russia as spy goes into hiding.

text.p: A Swedish defence industry worker, expelled from Russia for alleged spying, was suspended from his job on Thursday and went into hiding amid suggestions he was an undercover intelligence officer.
Peter Nordstrom, 32, and a senior Swedish diplomat were thrown out of Russia in February on spying accusations but the incident only surfaced on Wednesday in Russian newspapers.
Nordstrom, who works for aircraft technology group Celsius Tech, was at England's Farnborough airshow when the news broke and went into hiding after being tracked down by reporters.
Head of security at Celsius Tech, Lennart Ragvaldson, said the company had decided to suspend Nordstrom.
"He cannot come back again before this whole affair is cleared up," Ragvaldson told Swedish national news agency TT.

Swedish media said Nordstrom -- his name was originally spelled Nordstrem in Russian media -- was arrested in St Petersburg as he handed over $2,000 for a wooden doll containing film of secret documents. The exchange was filmed.
Nordstrom has denied any covert operation, telling reporters he was giving a friend money for a sick relative.
However MP Rolf Dahlberg, parliamentary head of an intelligence committee, told Swedish tabloid newspaper Expressen that Nordstrom was probably working as a "messenger" for the intelligence service.
"There was something in the spring about a reporter or what you call a messenger being arrested," Dahlberg said.
"It was the boss of intelligence that reported it to me and he said there had been a little incident."
Ragvaldson said Nordstrom was in Russia on private business and not on behalf of Celsius Tech earlier this year.
However he acknowledged that Nordstrom did work on classified material. Less than a year ago Nordstrom was given clearance during a security check by Sweden's security police.
Ragvaldson said it was surprising the company, which supplies some components for Sweden's JAS Gripen fighter jet, was kept in the dark over Nordstrom's expulsion from Russia.
"It's astonishing we never heard anything," he siad.
He told Expressen the whole affair could be a conspiracy by competitors trying to hinder sales of the JAS Gripen.
"(Our competitors) have saved this up until we were trying to sell the JAS," Ragvaldson said.
Opposition politicians were outraged at not being informed of the expulsions - even though Foreign Affairs Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen was told during a visit to Moscow in March.
A parliamentary foreign affairs committee was convened on Thursday involving all political party leaders who accused the government of trying to play down the affair.
Moscow said on Thursday the incident should not overshadow friendly relations between the two countries and no further action was planned.

"Taking into account the high level of Russo-Swedish relations reached in the recent years, the Russian side deemed it appropriate to limit its reaction to Nordstrom's expulsion," spokesman Mikhail Demurin said.
Demurin made clear the Swedish diplomat expelled over the incident had not been declared persona non grata in Russia.
